prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the enclosed 3D geometry of the narrow rock canyon, showing steep walls pressing in on the left and right (~1–3 m away) that recede into a deep, dark upper channel (~4–6 m away and several metres above). It clearly separates the camera wearer's bottom-cropped cell phone in the lower-left foreground (~0.3–0.5 m, within the wearer's arm's reach) from the backpack-wearing person standing in front and to the right (~0.8–1.2 m away, facing away and looking up the canyon) and the two side-by-side people standing high on the upper ledge (~4–6 m away, facing down toward the camera wearer in frames 1, 4, and 5). Across the five frames, the foreground person raises both arms to hold a phone overhead in frame 3 before dropping lower into the bottom-right frame in frames 4–5 while the camera wearer's phone shifts closer and higher in frame 5, partially occluding the lower mid-ground. Compared to RGB, the depth map makes the continuous distance gradient along the camouflaged rock walls and the sharp metric separation between the foreground silhouette and the canyon wall behind them immediately apparent. However, it is unreliable on the foreground phone screen—assigning deeper values to the 2D image displayed inside the bezel in frames 2 and 5—and produces overly bright, near-saturated artifacts at the top-left corner while nearly erasing the two distant upper-ledge people into the dark background.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates discrete foreground entities against the unlabelled canyon walls, identifying the camera wearer's bottom-cropped cell phone at the lower left (~0.3–0.5 m away, within arm's reach) and the nearby person (~0.8–1.2 m to the front-right, ~0.5–0.8 m from the wearer's phone) who faces away from the camera wearer while looking up the rock chute. In frames 2 and 3, it even segments the small 'person' reflection visible on the foreground phone screen (which faces toward the camera wearer), while in frame 3 it separates the foreground person's backpack straps and raised arms holding a second cell phone within their own reach (~1.0–1.3 m from the camera wearer). As the camera tilts upward in frames 4 and 5 and the foreground person drops lower at the bottom right, the map reveals the distant people standing side by side on the high ledge (~4–6 m away and ~3–5 m above the foreground person, facing toward the camera wearer) after they were cropped out in frames 2–3. Compared to RGB alone, the masks make the tiny raised cell phone in frames 3–4 and the small, shadowed upper-ledge hikers in frames 4–5 stand out clearly from the textured rock background. However, the map is unreliable in splitting the foreground person into overlapping 'person' and 'backpack' fragments in frame 3, missing their raised phone and backpack entirely in frame 5, and hallucinating a large 'dog' mask on the left rock wall and a 'car' label on the foreground cell phone in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is almost entirely blank across the sequence, rendering onlymagenta hand skeletons for the foreground person's raised left and right hands in frames 3 and 4 (~1.0–1.3 m in front of and slightly right of the camera wearer) and no yellow body skeletons in any frame. Using the RGB strip for context, those detected hands belong to the backpack-wearing person standing ~0.8–1.2 m away (facing away from the camera wearer and looking up the canyon) as they reach up with both arms to hold a small phone in frame 3 and lower it to head height in frame 4 before dropping further down in frame 5. The map fails to detect the camera wearer's own hands holding the bottom-cropped foreground phone (~0.3–0.5 m away), the face visible on that phone screen in frames 1–3, the foreground person's torso and head across all five frames, and the two distant people standing side by side on the upper rock ledge (~4–6 m away, facing the camera wearer in frames 1, 4, and 5). What the pose map does show that is harder to parse at a glance in the cluttered RGB rock textures is the exact 3D pinch-and-grip finger articulation and close inter-hand spacing (~0.05–0.10 m apart) of the foreground person's raised hands around their device in frames 3 and 4. Overall, the map is highly unreliable for scene-level spatial understanding because rear-facing orientation, clothing/backpack self-occlusion, bottom-edge cropping, and distance cause complete misses for every body skeleton and most visible limbs.
